questions.stem: Which combination best adapts a capillary for exchange?

options.text: A one-cell-thick wall, narrow lumen and extensively branched network
options.why: The thin wall shortens diffusion distance, the narrow lumen keeps blood close to it, and branching provides a large exchange area.

options.text: A thick muscular wall, narrow lumen and abundant elastic fibers
options.why: Those features adapt an artery to withstand and maintain high pressure. They would increase the distance across a capillary wall.

options.text: A thin flexible wall, wide lumen and regularly spaced pocket valves
options.why: Those are adaptations of veins for low-pressure return to the heart. Exchange vessels need a microscopic lumen and very thin wall.

options.text: A multilayered wall, wide lumen and complete covering of lignin
options.why: Lignin belongs to xylem vessels, while a multilayered wall would obstruct exchange between blood and tissues.

questions.stem: A blood vessel in a micrograph has a thick wall, a relatively narrow lumen and no visible valves. What is it most likely to be?

options.text: An artery carrying blood away from the heart
options.why: A thick wall containing muscle and elastin is suited to blood arriving from the heart at high pressure.

options.text: A vein returning blood to the heart at low pressure
options.why: A vein usually has a thinner wall, a wider lumen and may contain valves. It can also look collapsed in a section.

options.text: A capillary exchanging materials with surrounding cells
options.why: A capillary has a wall one endothelial cell thick. It doesn't have a thick muscular and elastic wall.

options.text: A lymph vessel draining excess fluid from tissues
options.why: Lymph vessels are thin-walled, low-pressure vessels with valves. The described wall fits an artery.

questions.stem: A student counts 18 radial pulse waves in 15 seconds. What pulse rate should be recorded?

options.text: 18 beats per minute
options.why: Eighteen is the count for only one quarter of a minute. It must be converted to a full minute.

options.text: 72 beats per minute
options.why: Fifteen seconds fits into one minute four times, so 18 is multiplied by four.

options.text: 270 beats per minute
options.why: Multiplying 18 by 15 uses the counting interval as a factor. The conversion factor is four.

options.text: 1.2 beats per minute
options.why: Dividing by 15 gives beats per second, not beats per minute. The requested unit requires conversion to 60 seconds.

questions.stem: What is the most direct consequence of complete occlusion of a coronary artery?

options.text: Cardiac muscle supplied by the artery receives less oxygen and may die
options.why: Coronary arteries supply cardiac muscle. A prolonged loss of blood flow can cause a myocardial infarction.

options.text: Blood can no longer return from the body through the vena cava
options.why: The venae cavae return systemic blood independently of the coronary artery. The blockage affects the heart muscle's own supply.

options.text: The lungs can no longer oxygenate blood in their capillaries
options.why: Gas exchange in lung capillaries isn't directly blocked. The immediate problem is ischemia in cardiac muscle.

options.text: The semilunar valves lose their ability to prevent arterial backflow
options.why: Semilunar valves respond to pressure differences. Coronary occlusion first deprives part of the myocardium of oxygen.

questions.stem: What generates the negative pressure that pulls water through xylem?

options.text: Active pumping of water by root cells
options.why: Root cells can actively transport ions, but water itself moves by osmosis. Transpiration pull doesn't require roots to pump water.

options.text: Evaporation of water from mesophyll cell walls
options.why: Evaporation draws water from leaf tissues and xylem, creating tension that is transmitted down the water column.

options.text: Cohesion between water molecules in the vessel
options.why: Cohesion keeps the water column connected and transmits tension. It doesn't create the tension.

options.text: Lignification of the xylem vessel walls
options.why: Lignin prevents the vessel from collapsing under tension. It isn't the source of transpiration pull.

questions.stem: Why are xylem vessel walls lignified?

options.text: To prevent collapse under tension and provide mechanical support
options.why: Lignin strengthens the walls, allowing the vessels to remain open while the water inside is under negative pressure.

options.text: To supply ATP for active transport of water through the lumen
options.why: Lignin is a structural material and mature vessels are dead. Xylem water transport is passive.

options.text: To form valves that prevent water from flowing toward the roots
options.why: Xylem vessels don't use valves. The transpiration-generated pressure gradient determines the direction of bulk flow.

options.text: To increase osmosis by lowering the water potential of the wall
options.why: Lignin doesn't act as a dissolved solute. Osmotic water movement depends on water-potential differences across membranes.

questions.stem: Which arrangement identifies a transverse section as a young dicotyledonous stem rather than a root?

options.text: Vascular bundles in a ring, with phloem outside and xylem inside each bundle
options.why: A young dicot stem has a ring of vascular bundles around the pith, with cambium between outer phloem and inner xylem.

options.text: Central star-shaped xylem, with phloem located between its projecting arms
options.why: That pattern identifies a young dicot root. Its vascular tissue occupies the central region rather than a ring of separate bundles.

options.text: Xylem around the outer epidermis, with phloem filling the central pith
options.why: Neither tissue occupies those positions in a normal young dicot stem. The epidermis remains the outer covering.

options.text: Phloem inside every xylem group, with no cortex outside the vascular tissue
options.why: Phloem is outside the xylem in each stem bundle, and cortex lies between the epidermis and vascular bundles.

questions.stem: Why do most plasma proteins remain in a capillary while tissue fluid forms?

options.text: They are too large to pass readily through the capillary wall
options.why: Pressure filters water and small solutes out, while most proteins remain in plasma and contribute to its osmotic pull.

options.text: They are actively transported from tissue fluid back into the capillary
options.why: Their retention is mainly due to the capillary barrier, not continuous active transport from the tissues.

options.text: They dissolve in red blood cells before reaching the arterial end
options.why: Plasma proteins remain dissolved in plasma. They don't move into red blood cells to avoid filtration.

options.text: They are converted into glucose as hydrostatic pressure increases
options.why: Hydrostatic pressure drives filtration but doesn't chemically convert proteins into glucose.

questions.stem: What happens to excess tissue fluid that doesn't return directly to blood capillaries?

options.text: It enters lymph vessels and later returns to veins near the heart
options.why: Lymphatic drainage prevents fluid from accumulating in tissues and eventually returns the fluid to the blood circulation.

options.text: It enters arteries and returns directly to the left ventricle
options.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and aren't open drainage routes for tissue fluid.

options.text: It remains permanently between cells to maintain hydrostatic pressure
options.why: Permanent accumulation would cause edema and interfere with exchange. Excess fluid must be drained.

options.text: It diffuses through body cells and leaves through the digestive tract
options.why: Tissue fluid exchanges solutes with cells, but excess bulk fluid is collected by lymphatic vessels.

questions.stem: Why can a mammalian double circulation deliver blood to the body at higher pressure than a fish single circulation?

options.text: Blood returning from the lungs is pumped again before entering systemic arteries
options.why: The left side of the mammalian heart re-pressurizes blood after pulmonary capillaries before sending it around the body.

options.text: Mammalian blood avoids capillaries until it has passed through every body organ
options.why: Systemic exchange still occurs through capillaries. Re-pressurization after the pulmonary circuit explains the higher pressure.

options.text: Fish blood returns to the heart between the gills and every individual organ
options.why: Fish blood travels from gills to body tissues before returning to the heart, which is why pressure isn't restored after the gills.

options.text: Mammalian veins generate a second pressure wave by contracting their muscular walls
options.why: Veins don't provide the second pump. Ventricular contraction in the heart generates arterial pressure.

questions.stem: Which valve state is expected while ventricular pressure exceeds both atrial and arterial pressure?

options.text: Atrioventricular valves open and semilunar valves closed
options.why: That arrangement occurs during ventricular filling. High ventricular pressure closes the atrioventricular valves.

options.text: Atrioventricular valves closed and semilunar valves open
options.why: Pressure above atrial pressure closes the inlet valves, while pressure above arterial pressure opens the outlet valves.

options.text: Both sets of valves open to maximize ventricular flow
options.why: Opening both sets would allow backward movement into the atria during contraction. The atrioventricular valves must be closed.

options.text: Both sets of valves closed throughout ventricular ejection
options.why: Both sets close briefly during isovolumetric contraction, but semilunar valves open when ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes electrical conduction during a normal heartbeat?

options.text: Atrioventricular node → atria → sinoatrial node → ventricles
options.why: The sinoatrial node starts the signal. The atrioventricular node receives it only after excitation spreads across the atria.

options.text: Sinoatrial node → atria → atrioventricular node → ventricular conducting fibers
options.why: The sinoatrial node initiates atrial excitation, and the delayed signal then travels through conducting tissue to the ventricles.

options.text: Ventricular muscle → semilunar valves → atria → sinoatrial node
options.why: Valves don't conduct electrical signals, and ventricular contraction follows atrial excitation rather than initiating it.

options.text: Coronary arteries → sinoatrial node → valves → ventricular muscle
options.why: Coronary arteries supply the myocardium but aren't part of its electrical conduction pathway. Valves aren't conducting tissue either.

questions.stem: How does active transport of mineral ions lead to root pressure?

options.text: It raises xylem water potential, causing water to leave and pull sap upward
options.why: Adding ions lowers xylem water potential. Water then enters rather than leaves.

options.text: It lowers xylem water potential, so osmosis adds water and creates positive pressure
options.why: Water entering the confined xylem produces positive hydrostatic pressure, especially when transpiration is low.

options.text: It pumps water molecules through ion channels and into xylem vessels
options.why: Ion pumps transport ions using ATP. Water follows passively by osmosis rather than being pumped through ion channels.

options.text: It creates negative xylem pressure by increasing evaporation from root cells
options.why: Root pressure is positive and comes from osmotic water entry. Negative pressure is associated with transpiration from leaves.

questions.stem: What directly drives long-distance mass flow of phloem sap from a source toward a sink?

options.text: Continuous active transport of each sucrose molecule along the sieve tube
options.why: ATP is involved in loading and unloading, but sucrose isn't pumped from cell to cell for the whole journey.

options.text: A hydrostatic pressure gradient produced by loading and unloading solutes
options.why: Sucrose loading draws water into phloem and raises pressure at the source, while unloading helps maintain lower pressure at the sink.

options.text: Transpiration tension transmitted from xylem through every sieve plate
options.why: Transpiration produces negative pressure in xylem. Phloem mass flow uses positive hydrostatic pressure.

options.text: Contraction of companion cells around each living sieve tube element
options.why: Companion cells support loading and metabolism but don't contract to squeeze sap along the tube.
